text:
Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (CFS), also called Myalgic Encephalomyelitis (ME), is a complex, long-term illness whose hallmark is overwhelming fatigue that isn’t improved by rest and is severe enough to interfere with daily life.

Key points to know:

1. Core symptoms  
   • Persistent, unexplained fatigue lasting ≥ 6 months  
   • Post-exertional malaise (PEM): a marked worsening of symptoms after even minor physical or mental activity, often delayed by hours or a day and lasting days or weeks  
   • Unrefreshing sleep

2. Additional common symptoms  
   • Cognitive difficulties (“brain fog”)—problems with memory, attention, word-finding  
   • Orthostatic intolerance—dizziness, light-headedness, or rapid heartbeat when standing  
   • Muscle or joint pain without swelling or redness  
   • Headaches of a new type or severity  
   • Sore throat or tender lymph nodes

3. Possible causes (still under study)  
   • Viral or bacterial infections (e.g., EBV, CMV, COVID-19, Lyme)  
   • Immune system dysregulation  
   • Hormonal/endocrine abnormalities  
   • Autonomic nervous system dysfunction  
   • Genetic susceptibility and environmental triggers

4. Diagnosis  
   • There is no single diagnostic test. Doctors rule out other conditions (anemia, thyroid disorders, depression, sleep apnea, etc.) through history, physical exam, and basic labs.  
   • Most guidelines use clinical criteria such as the 2015 U.S. Institute of Medicine (now NAM) definition: 6 months of disabling fatigue plus PEM, unrefreshing sleep, and either cognitive impairment or orthostatic intolerance.

5. Management and treatment  
   • Pacing & energy management: planning activity to avoid triggering PEM (often using heart-rate monitors or the “energy envelope” concept).  
   • Sleep hygiene: consistent schedule, dark quiet bedroom, limiting caffeine/alcohol; medication only if needed.  
   • Treat co-existing conditions: migraines, orthostatic intolerance (e.g., increased salt/fluid, compression garments, medications like fludrocortisone or midodrine), pain, depression/anxiety.  
   • Physical activity is individualized; graded exercise therapy is no longer broadly recommended because it can worsen PEM.  
   • Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) may help some patients cope but is not a cure.  
   • Emerging/experimental options: low-dose naltrexone, antiviral or immunomodulatory drugs in select cases, and ongoing research on metabolic and immune-targeted therapies.

6. Prognosis  
   • Course is variable: some improve over time, others remain stable or worsen. Full recovery is uncommon but significant symptom improvement is possible, especially with good pacing and comorbidity management.

7. When to seek medical help  
   • Any new, persistent fatigue not explained by lifestyle or clearly reversible causes.  
   • Worsening symptoms, thinking or memory changes, or signs of depression or anxiety.  
   • Difficulty standing or frequent pre-syncope/syncope.

Self-help resources  
   • ME/CFS support groups (online and local)  
   • CDC ME/CFS information pages  
   • ME Association, Solve ME/CFS Initiative, Long Covid & ME/CFS clinics (for post-viral cases)
